claims.text: The proposed approach explicitly separates lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr.
High-purity, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr has a lattice thermal conductivity of about 6 W/(K·m), with an uncertainty of ±1 W/(K·m).
The lattice thermal conductivity of high-purity HfNbTaTiZr remains nearly constant from 50 to 300 K.
The electronic thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr increases approximately linearly with temperature.
The proposed model will reproduce experimental total-conductivity trends.
The proposed model will reduce total-conductivity prediction error by roughly 50% relative to earlier approaches.
Effective-temperature scaling can represent the effects of static and dynamic lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Effective-temperature scaling captures force-constant disorder relevant to thermal transport.
Local lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations dominate phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Static lattice distortions alter phonon lifetimes in a way that can be modeled by an effective-temperature scaling law.
Combining effective-temperature scaling with ab initio electronic-scattering calculations accounts separately for disorder effects on phonon and electron transport.
Arc melting followed by homogenization annealing can produce nearly single-phase, defect-minimized HfNbTaTiZr with less than 1 wt.% oxygen.
Earlier analytical and ab initio approaches treated defect-free perfect crystals and used Debye-temperature approximations while conflating lattice and electronic transport.
Earlier approaches often overestimated electronic compensation in high-resistivity states.
The model is applicable to nearly defect-free HfNbTaTiZr containing less than 1 wt.% oxygen.
Secondary phases, oxidation, microsegregation, and grain-boundary defects can place samples outside the model's applicability domain.
Concurrent electrical-resistivity measurements and the Wiedemann–Franz law can be used to estimate the electronic contribution for falsification testing.
Residual defects, microsegregation, and imperfect treatment of electron–phonon coupling may cause deviations from the prediction.
